## Why bother separating them: a crime based illustration

Two neighbourhoods record the same number of homicides over a year. In one,
the events are spread through the year with no particular relationship to each
other: the place is simply dangerous, for reasons that were true before any of 
those events and remain true after, e.g. land use, guardianship,
who passes through. In the other, one shooting was followed by a retaliation, 
which was followed by another, all within weeks and within close proximity.

The count is identical. The right response is not. The first calls for
sustained structural work; the second calls for rapid, targeted disruption of
a chain that is currently running. A model that reports only intensity cannot
tell them apart. That is the whole reason for fitting a self-exciting process
rather than an inhomogeneous Poisson one.

This article shows how to get that separation out of a fitted model.

```{r setup}
library(spHawkes)
library(sf)
```

## The two components

The fitted conditional intensity has exactly two terms:

$$
\lambda(x, y, t \mid H_t) \;=\;
\underbrace{\mu_0\, \mu_T(t)\, \mu_m(t)\, \mu_w(t)\, \mu_b(x, y)}_{\text{background}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{A \sum_{i:\, t_i < t} g(t - t_i)\, h(x - x_i,\, y - y_i)}_{\text{triggering}}
$$

Accumulating each over a time window $\mathcal{T}$ gives two surfaces that add
up to the total risk over that period:

$$
\Lambda_\mathcal{T}(x,y) \;=\; \Lambda^{\text{bg}}_\mathcal{T}(x,y) \;+\; \Lambda^{\text{tr}}_\mathcal{T}(x,y)
$$

$\Lambda^{\text{bg}}$ is the geography of persistent risk — where events are
expected regardless of what has just happened. $\Lambda^{\text{tr}}$ is the
part attributable to the events that actually occurred.

## Fitting

We use the bundled simulated data (`?sim_events`), which was generated with
a known branching ratio of `A = 0.35`. The fit limits the triggering kernel
to 1 km from each event (`trigger_window_dist` and the kernel grid's
`x_range`), a few times the distance at which the simulation placed
offspring. A much wider reach lets the kernel's tail absorb clustering in
the background and inflates `A`.

```{r fit, results = "hide"}
fit <- fit_semihawkes(
  points    = sim_events,
  region    = sim_region,
  date_col  = "date",
  cell_size = 400,
  cache_dir = tempfile("spHawkes_marks_"),
  bandwidth_args = list(k = 5, min_dist = 150, min_bandwidth = 300),
  trigger_window_dist  = 1000,
  trigger_spatial_args = list(x_range = 1000),
  n_iter    = 12,
  verbose   = FALSE
)
```

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The summary already gives the split *overall* — what share of events the model
attributes to each mechanism. What it does not give is **where**.

## Computing the two surfaces

Everything needed is on the fitted object. The background is a product of the
temporal multipliers and the spatial surface; the triggering term is a sum over
observed events of the two kernels.

```{r decompose}
grid_x <- fit$background$x
grid_y <- fit$background$y
ev     <- fit$events$events
days   <- seq(0, floor(fit$events$TT))          # daily bins over the study period

# Background: separable, so the time factors collapse to a single scalar.
time_factor <- sum(fit$trend$fun(days) *
                   fit$weekly$fun(days) *
                   fit$monthly$fun(days))
Lambda_bg <- fit$mu * time_factor * fit$background$basevalue

# Triggering: accumulate each event's kernel over the grid.
GX <- grid_x %o% rep(1, length(grid_y))
GY <- rep(1, length(grid_x)) %o% grid_y

Lambda_tr <- matrix(0, nrow = length(grid_x), ncol = length(grid_y))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(ev))) {
  g_sum <- sum(fit$temporal_trigger$fun(days - ev$days[i]))
  if (g_sum <= 0) next
  Lambda_tr <- Lambda_tr +
    g_sum * fit$spatial_trigger$fun(GX - ev$coorx[i], GY - ev$coory[i])
}
Lambda_tr <- fit$A * Lambda_tr
```

Mask to the study region, and check the split against what `summary()` reported:

```{r check}
in_region <- fit$background$marks > 0
Lambda_bg[!in_region] <- NA
Lambda_tr[!in_region] <- NA

share_triggering <- sum(Lambda_tr, na.rm = TRUE) /
  sum(Lambda_bg + Lambda_tr, na.rm = TRUE)
round(share_triggering, 3)
```

This lands close to the `summary()` figure above, which is a reassuring
cross-check — but note that the two are *related, not identical*, quantities.
`summary()` averages the fitted probability that each **observed event** was
triggered; the number here is the share of **accumulated intensity** over the
whole region attributable to the triggering term. They answer slightly
different questions and need not agree exactly. Landing within a percentage
point of each other is evidence that neither computation has gone wrong; it is
not an algebraic identity.

```{r totals, include = FALSE}
# Expected number of events implied by the two surfaces, for the text below.
expected_total <- sum(Lambda_bg + Lambda_tr, na.rm = TRUE) *
  diff(grid_x[1:2]) * diff(grid_y[1:2])
```

The *absolute* totals are less exact. Added up, the two surfaces imply about
`r round(expected_total)` events against the `r nrow(ev)` observed, because
this is a coarse Riemann sum over grid cells and whole days whereas the
package integrates on a finer temporal mesh internally. Read the proportions
rather than the totals.

## Where each mechanism dominates

```{r maps, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.3, echo = FALSE}
Lambda_total <- Lambda_bg + Lambda_tr

# The share is unstable where there is almost no risk at all: a tiny
# triggering contribution over a tiny background is a large ratio and means
# nothing. Show it only for the more active half of the region.
share <- Lambda_tr / Lambda_total
share[Lambda_total < median(Lambda_total, na.rm = TRUE)] <- NA

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 5.5), cex.main = 1.05)
fields::image.plot(grid_x, grid_y, Lambda_bg, main = "Background",
                   xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "y (m)",
                   col = hcl.colors(64, "Blues", rev = TRUE))
fields::image.plot(grid_x, grid_y, Lambda_tr, main = "Triggering",
                   xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "",
                   col = hcl.colors(64, "Greens 3", rev = TRUE))
fields::image.plot(grid_x, grid_y, share, main = "Triggering share",
                   xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "",
                   col = hcl.colors(64, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE))
par(op)
```

The first two panels look similar, and they should: triggered events happen
near where events happen, so both components peak in the same three places.

The third panel is the one that carries information the first two do not. It
is the *proportion* of accumulated risk attributable to triggering, shown only
where there is enough risk for the ratio to mean something. Low values mark
places whose risk is structural — they would be dangerous regardless. High
values mark places whose risk is disproportionately a consequence of recent
events, and where interrupting the chain is therefore the intervention with
something to bite on.

In the paper's vocabulary, the low-share cores are **established** hotspots
and the high-share margins are **emerging** ones.

## Reading it with care

Three caveats worth carrying.

**The share is a ratio, and ratios mislead where the denominator is small.**
Hence the masking above. Without it, the highest triggering shares appear in
the emptiest parts of the map, which is an artefact rather than a finding.

**This is a fixed window.** Both surfaces were accumulated over the whole
study period. Computing them year by year is what turns this into the paper's
account of hotspots that shift and reorganise, and is a matter of restricting
`days` and the event set to each window in turn.

**Attribution is model-based, not observed.** The branching structure is
latent. "This cell is 40% triggered" means the fitted model assigns 40% of the
accumulated intensity there to the self-exciting term — under this
specification of the background. A background specified differently would
move that number, which is exactly why the background's form is a substantive
modelling decision rather than a default.

## A note on where this is going

The loop above is deliberately written out rather than hidden, because it is
short and because seeing it makes clear what the decomposition actually is.
It is, however, the obvious candidate for a `predict()` method — one that
takes a fit, a period and a component and returns the surface directly. Doing
it here first fixes the output and the interface in a form that can be
critiqued before any of it is committed to the package's API.
